eras.name: Navigational
eras.background: The first database systems, such as IBM's IMS, stored business records in trees or networks of links. Programs walked those links one record at a time, so changes to the structure often meant rewriting them.

eras.name: Relational
eras.background: Codd proposed storing data as tables and letting the system find it, which set off a long debate. IBM's System R and Berkeley's INGRES then showed such systems could run efficiently, and System R introduced SQL.

eras.name: Commercial SQL
eras.background: IBM's DB2 ended the debate, and SQL products from IBM, Oracle and others came to run business data. Vendors kept one engine design for every workload, while research hardened it with better recovery and new data types.

eras.name: Specialized engines
eras.background: Stonebraker argued that one engine built for business transactions no longer fit every market. Analytics moved to engines that store and process data by column, while web developers adopted document stores.

eras.name: Embedded analytics
eras.background: Data scientists analyzed files in R and Python, whose tools lacked full query optimization. Analytic databases ran as separate servers that took effort to set up, so engines moved into the analyst's own process.

nodes.label: IMS and CODASYL
nodes.problem: Each business built its own tools to store and update shared data.
nodes.idea: IMS stores records in trees and CODASYL in networks, which programs walk a record at a time.
nodes.impact: IMS became the database of choice across industries, but programs were tied to its structure.

nodes.label: Relational model
nodes.idea: Codd represents all data as tables of values, with no links visible to programs.
nodes.impact: Separated what data means from how it is stored, and set off a long debate.

from.why: Programs depended on stored trees and pointers, so reorganizing the data broke them.

nodes.label: B-tree
nodes.problem: Indexes on disk had to stay cheap to search while records were inserted and deleted.
nodes.idea: Bayer and McCreight keep a balanced tree of wide nodes that split as they fill.
nodes.impact: Within a decade it was the standard index structure in database systems.

nodes.label: Two-phase locking
nodes.problem: Concurrent users could interleave updates and leave shared data inconsistent.
nodes.idea: IBM researchers require each transaction to take no new lock once it releases one.
nodes.impact: Interleaved transactions then behave as if run one at a time, and most SQL products used locking.

nodes.label: MVCC
nodes.idea: Keep several versions of each item, so readers see a snapshot while writers add new ones.
nodes.impact: Oracle and Postgres adopted it early, and almost every new engine now uses it.

from.why: Under locking, readers and writers of the same data had to wait for each other.

nodes.label: System R
nodes.idea: IBM's prototype pairs the SQL language with an optimizer that picks plans by estimated cost.
nodes.impact: SQL became the de facto standard, and many commercial optimizers adopted its methods.

from.why: Skeptics doubted a system could choose query plans as well as a skilled programmer.

nodes.label: Postgres
nodes.idea: Stonebraker's Postgres lets users add their own data types, operators and index methods.
nodes.impact: Extensible relational systems outlasted object databases, and the code became PostgreSQL.

from.why: Engines hard-wired a few business data types, so maps and other new data fit badly.

nodes.label: ARIES
nodes.problem: Each system recovered from crashes with its own complex, ad hoc method.
nodes.idea: Pair write-ahead logging with one recipe: after a crash, repeat history from the log, then undo unfinished work.
nodes.impact: Most commercial engines, SQL Server included, still recover this way.

nodes.label: LSM-tree
nodes.idea: Buffer writes in memory, then merge them into sorted runs on disk in batches.
nodes.impact: RocksDB, forked from Google's LevelDB, now runs it under many databases and stream processors.

from.why: Under heavy inserts, keeping a B-tree index current cost many random disk writes.

nodes.label: C-Store
nodes.idea: Store each column separately and compressed, so a query reads only the columns it needs.
nodes.impact: Became Vertica, and warehouse vendors have since moved from row stores to column stores.

from.why: Engines stored whole rows together, so analytic scans read columns they did not need.

nodes.label: MonetDB/X100
nodes.problem: Engines passed one row at a time between operators, wasting modern CPUs on overhead.
nodes.idea: Operators work on small, cache-resident vectors of column values instead of single rows.
nodes.impact: Spun out as Vectorwise, and vectorized execution became a mainstream engine design.

nodes.label: Document stores
nodes.idea: Systems such as MongoDB store schemaless JSON documents behind a simple, record-at-a-time API.
nodes.impact: Within about a decade nearly all had added SQL, and the SQL standard had added JSON.

from.why: SQL databases struggled to scale for web apps, whose developers saw joins as slow and schemas as rigid.

nodes.label: DuckDB
nodes.idea: Like SQLite, it runs inside the host process, but stores columns and executes in vectors.
nodes.impact: Grew popular, partly because it queries local and cloud files in place.

from.why: Supplied the vectorized execution that DuckDB's engine adopted.
Fast column stores ran as servers that took effort to set up and load.

main.title: CMU 15-445/645: Intro to Database Systems
main.why: Storage, indexes, query execution and optimization, concurrency control and recovery. In English.

main.title: Architecture of a Database System
main.why: How real databases handle processes, memory and parallelism, which textbooks skip.

main.title: Evolution of Development Priorities in Key-value Stores Serving Large-scale Applications: The RocksDB Experience
main.why: RocksDB's priorities shifted from write amplification to space to CPU as its hardware and workloads changed.

main.title: The Part of PostgreSQL We Hate the Most
main.why: Postgres MVCC copies the whole row on each update, causing bloat and vacuum pain.

further.title: Yes, PostgreSQL Has Problems. But We're Sticking With It!

main.title: An Overview of Query Optimization in Relational Systems
main.why: SQL leaves the plan to the system, and this survey explains how optimizers search and cost plans, starting from System R.

main.title: How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really?
main.why: Cardinality estimates are often far off and matter more than the cost model, as the Join Order Benchmark shows.

main.title: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels
main.why: The ANSI isolation levels are defined too vaguely, and the paper adds snapshot isolation, which still allows write skew.

main.title: Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases
main.why: Snapshot isolation still allows write skew, so SSI detects dangerous patterns at runtime and aborts a transaction, as PostgreSQL does.

main.title: C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS
main.why: Analytic queries read a few columns of many rows, so C-Store stores data by column and reads only what a query needs.

main.title: MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution
main.why: Row-at-a-time execution wastes CPU on interpretation, so X100's vectorized operators process a batch of values per call.

main.title: DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database
main.why: Analysts needed fast analytics inside their own process, so DuckDB is embedded like SQLite but columnar and vectorized.

main.title: What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around...
main.why: Many data models tried to replace SQL, and this retrospective shows how SQL and the relational model absorbed their best ideas.
Altering a busy MySQL table can block writes, so online migration tools copy it to a shadow table in the background and swap it in.
Postgres uses one process per connection, so Figma built a pooler that sheds load.
VIP and DNS based failover was slow and fragile, so GitHub uses orchestrator to promote a replica and Consul with GLB to route clients to it.
GitHub upgraded its whole MySQL fleet in stages, replicas first, while replicating back to the old version so it could roll back.
Notion's single Postgres was nearing its limits, so it split the data into logical shards by workspace and migrated with double writes.
